Jane admitted that the engagement surprised her a little, but she spoke less of her surprise than of her heartfelt wish for their happiness. Elizabeth could not persuade her that such happiness was unlikely. Kitty and Lydia felt no envy of Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins was merely a clergyman. To them the engagement meant nothing beyond a piece of news to circulate in Meryton.

Lady Lucas could hardly avoid a sense of triumph now that she could answer Mrs. Bennet's boasts with the comfort of seeing her own daughter marry well. She visited Longbourn somewhat more often than usual to announce her happiness, although Mrs. Bennet's sour expressions and unkind remarks might have been enough to extinguish it.

An awkwardness between Elizabeth and Charlotte kept both of them silent on the subject. Elizabeth was convinced that they could never truly confide in each other again. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her turn more affectionately toward her sister, whose integrity and sensitivity, she felt certain, could never fail her. Her anxiety for Jane's happiness increased each day: Bingley had now been away a week, and there was no news of his return.

Jane had answered Caroline's letter promptly and was counting the days until she could reasonably expect another. Mr. Collins's promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father. Its solemn gratitude might have been appropriate after a full year's stay with the family. Having satisfied his conscience on that point, he went on, in delighted language, to describe his happiness at winning the affection of their charming neighbour, Miss Lucas. He then explained that the sole reason he had so readily accepted their kind invitation to return to Longbourn was to enjoy her company. He hoped to arrive two weeks from Monday, because Lady Catherine, he added, approved of his marriage so enthusiastically that she wanted it celebrated as soon as possible. He trusted this would provide an irresistible argument for his dear Charlotte to choose an early date for making him the happiest of men.

Mrs. Bennet no longer looked forward to Mr. Collins's return to Hertfordshire. On the contrary, she was now as inclined to complain about it as her husband. Why should he come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge? It was very strange, as well as highly inconvenient and extremely troublesome. She hated having visitors when her health was so poor, and people in love were the most disagreeable visitors of all.

"I cannot say how long I remained in that condition. It must have been quite some time, though, because when I partly regained consciousness, daylight was breaking. The balloon hung at an incredible height above an empty expanse of ocean, with no trace of land anywhere along the vast horizon. Yet coming to my senses caused far less anguish than might have been expected. In fact, the calmness with which I began assessing my position suggested the beginnings of madness. I raised first one hand and then the other before my eyes, wondering what could have caused the veins to swell and the fingernails to turn such a dreadful black. Next I carefully examined my head, shaking it several times and feeling it all over with meticulous attention, until I was satisfied that it was not, as I had rather suspected, larger than my balloon. Then, with an air of knowing exactly what I was doing, I felt in both pockets of my trousers. My writing tablets and toothpick case were missing. I tried to explain their disappearance, and when I could not, I felt indescribably annoyed. Only then did I notice a severe discomfort in my left ankle, and a faint understanding of my predicament began to emerge. Strangely enough, I felt neither astonishment nor horror. If I felt anything, it was a sort of amused satisfaction at the cleverness I was about to demonstrate in getting myself out of this difficulty. Not for one moment did I consider my eventual safety uncertain. For several minutes I remained immersed in intense thought. I distinctly recall repeatedly pressing my lips together, placing my forefinger beside my nose, and making the other gestures and faces of a man who ponders complex or important matters from the comfort of his armchair. Once I thought I had sufficiently organized my ideas, I reached behind my back with great care and deliberation and undid the large iron buckle on my trouser waistband. It had three prongs, which were somewhat rusty and turned only with considerable difficulty on their pivot. After some effort, however, I managed to set them at right angles to the buckle, and was pleased to find that they stayed firmly in place. Holding this newly fashioned tool between my teeth, I began untying the knot of my neckcloth. I had to stop and rest several times before I could finish the task, but eventually it was done.

A great many American ladies, upon quitting their own country, assume a look of habitual invalidism, believing it to mark European elegance; Mrs. Otis, however, had never made this mistake. Her constitution was superb, and her stock of high spirits truly extraordinary. Indeed, she was thoroughly English in several respects, admirably illustrating how much we now share with America in everything save, naturally, our language. Her eldest boy, named Washington during a patriotic moment which his parents bestowed upon him and he never ceased regretting, was a blond, fairly handsome young man. Three consecutive seasons of leading the German at the Newport Casino had prepared him for American diplomacy, and even London knew him as a first-rate dancer. His only frailties were gardenias and the aristocracy; in other matters he was remarkably sensible. Miss Virginia E. Otis, a small girl of fifteen, was graceful and lovely as a young deer, with a splendid independence in her great blue eyes. An admirable horsewoman, she had once ridden her pony twice around the park against old Lord Bilton, beating him by a length and a half just before the Achilles statue. This so delighted the young Duke of Cheshire that he offered marriage immediately, whereupon his guardians sent him back to Eton that same evening, weeping copiously. After Virginia came the twins, generally styled 'The Stars and Stripes,' because they were so frequently caned. They were charming boys and, apart from the worthy Minister, the family's sole genuine republicans.

Canterville Chase stood seven miles from Ascot, its nearest railway station, so Mr. Otis had wired for a waggonette to collect them. They began the drive in excellent spirits. The July evening was beautiful, the air delicately scented by pine woods. Occasionally they heard a wood pigeon lingering over its own melodious notes, or glimpsed a pheasant's gleaming breast among the whispering ferns. Little squirrels watched their passage from the beeches, while rabbits darted through the undergrowth and across moss-covered hillocks, white tails raised. On their entering the avenue to Canterville Chase, however, clouds abruptly spread across the sky. An odd hush settled upon the air, a great flock of rooks flew soundlessly overhead, and several heavy raindrops had fallen before they reached the house.

An elderly woman waited upon the steps to welcome them, neatly attired in black silk with a white apron and cap.
